paper_title: High-Fidelity Image Matting with Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion models have shown strong potential for image matting by transferring generative priors learned from large-scale pretraining. However, existing approaches largely rely on latent diffusion models, whose compressed representations and VAE-based reconstruction introduce a mismatch with the high-frequency precision required for matting. We present PixelMatte, a framework that adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers for high-fidelity image matting. We show that strong image-conditioned matting capabilities can be acquired even from a pure text-to-image model without paired image-to-image pretraining. Our approach reuses the backbone's native patch embedding to jointly process the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte as spatially aligned tokens, enabling direct pixel-space prediction without additional condition encoders or adapters. With pixel-accurate synthetic supervision and real-image fine-tuning, PixelMatte predicts alpha mattes in a single forward pass. Two lightweight calibration modules, LayerShift and High-Pass Refiner, further improve regional opacity accuracy and boundary fidelity. Experiments across four benchmarks and two distinct pixel diffusion backbones demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods, reducing SAD and gradient errors by 24-44% relative to RenderMatte on P3M-500-NP and AM-2K, while achieving competitive performance on AIM-500 and RenderMatte-2K. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pixel-space generative priors for precision-sensitive image matting. Project page: https://white-yc.github.io/pixelmatte/.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion models have shown strong potential for image matting by transferring generative priors learned from large-scale pretraining. However, existing approaches largely rely on latent diffusion models, whose compressed representations and VAE-based reconstruction introduce mismatch with the high-frequency precision required for matting. We present PixelMatte, framework that adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers for high-fidelity image matting. We show that strong imageconditioned matting capabilities can be acquired even from pure text-to-image model without paired image-to-image pretraining. Our approach reuses the backbones native patch embedding to jointly process the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte as spatially aligned tokens, enabling direct pixel-space prediction without additional condition encoders or adapters. With pixel-accurate synthetic supervision and real-image fine-tuning, PixelMatte predicts alpha mattes in single forward pass. Two lightweight calibration modules, LayerShift and High-Pass Refiner, further improve regional opacity accuracy and boundary fidelity. Experiments across four benchmarks and two distinct pixel diffusion backbones demonstrate substantial improvements over existing methods, reducing SAD and gradient errors by 2444% relative to RenderMatte on P3M-500NP and AM-2K, while achieving competitive performance on AIM-500 and RenderMatte-2K. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of pixel-space generative priors for precision-sensitive image matting. Project page: https: //white-yc.github.io/pixelmatte/. 1. Introduction Image matting estimates the per-pixel alpha matte of an arbitrary foreground object from the observed image [17]. Unlike traditional image segmentation, which assigns dis1 crete labels, image matting is an inherently ill-posed inverse problem due to the ambiguity in recovering alpha values from composite image [9, 33, 41]. Trimap-guided matting addresses this ambiguity by introducing an auxiliary trimap that partitions the image into definite foreground, definite background, and an unknown region requiring exact alpha estimation. The trimaps may be produced using segmentation models [12, 18, 50], providing semantic and spatial guidance for image matting models to focus on recovering fine-grained details within the unknown region. The main challenge lies in intricate structures such as hair, fur, foliage, and transparent boundaries, where accurate alpha estimation requires pixel-level precision. Traditionally, image matting has been formulated as supervised regression problem [5, 8, 21, 25, 27, 29, 31, 39, 44, 46]. More recently, generative approaches have emerged that adapt pretrained diffusion models for alpha matte prediction [6, 9, 33, 41, 45, 47]. These methods leverage rich generative priors acquired through large-scale pretraining, which can help mitigate the effects of imperfect alpha annotations and enable generalization to diverse visual content beyond the limited distributions of existing matting datasets. However, most existing generative approaches rely on latent diffusion models [13, 34], creating an inherent mismatch with the pixel-level precision required for image matting. Matting is high-frequency task, yet the network of latent model operates on spatially compressed representation in which hair-thin structures and opacity tranIt presitions are not represented explicitly [4, 48, 49]. dicts compressed code and is supervised at the pixel level only through frozen decoder trained for natural images [20, 42, 43, 51]. Fine details are therefore recovered indirectly, relying on the strength of the generative prior rather than on direct modeling of high-frequency alpha structure. Recent advances in pixel-space diffusion models have made high-quality image generation directly in pixel space increasingly practical, enabled by improved prediction objectives, architectures, and training strategies [2, 19, 23, 24, 32, 48]. In contrast to latent diffusion models, these approaches bypass VAE-based compression and reconstruction, preserving direct access to high-frequency image information that is only implicitly encoded in latent representations. This enables diffusion transformers to learn and optimize fine-grained visual structures under direct pixelspace supervision, making them particularly promising for image matting, where precise recovery of high-frequency details is essential. In this paper, we present PixelMatte, simple yet effective framework for high-fidelity matting built upon pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers. We demonstrate that even pure text-to-image model without paired imageto-image pretraining can acquire strong image-conditioned matting capabilities through supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, we directly embed the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte using the backbones native patch embedding, enabling spatially aligned conditioning without additional encoders or adapters. We adapt the pretrained models using the pixel-accurate synthetic training data of RenderMatte [33], followed by mixed training with real images. We further introduce two lightweight calibration modules, LayerShift and High-Pass Refiner, to improve opacity accuracy and boundary fidelity, respectively. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce PixelMatte, framework that adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers to image matting by reusing the backbones native patch embedding for spatially aligned image and trimap conditioning. It needs no VAE, condition encoder or adapter, predicts the matte in single step, and works even for pure text-toimage backbone (PRXPixel [32]) without paired imageto-image pretraining. We propose two lightweight calibration modules: LayerShift, learned per-layer shifts that adjust regional opacity levels inside the frozen backbone, and the High-Pass Refiner, small high-pass-constrained residual network that sharpens boundary transitions. With two pixel diffusion backbones, PixelMatte achieves state-of-the-art results on P3M-500-NP and AM-2K, reducing the SAD of RenderMatte [33] from 6.2 to 4.3 and from 6.5 to 4.4, and competitive results on AIM-500 and RenderMatte-2K. 2. Related Work Trimap-guided matting. Deep Image Matting [44] established learning-based framework for trimap-guided alpha estimation and introduced the Composition-1k benchmark. Subsequent methods improved alpha regression through learned feature indexing [29], guided contextual attention [21], attention-based representations [31], and pretrained vision transformers with detail-capture modules [46]. Real-image datasets, including P3M-10k [14], AM-2K [16], and AIM-500 [15], have further advanced the evaluation of matting in diverse natural scenes. These approaches primarily learn direct alpha regression from matting-specific supervision, with high-frequency details recovered through task-specific architectures and image features. In contrast, PixelMatte explores transferring pretrained pixel-space generative priors to fine-grained alpha prediction. Generative priors for image matting. The success of pretrained diffusion models has motivated their adaptation to dense visual prediction tasks [7, 11, 30, 35, 43]. In image matting, Matting by Generation [41] formulates alpha estimation as conditional generation using pretrained latent 2 Figure 2. Overview of PixelMatte. (a) Latent diffusion matting predicts the matte as latent code between frozen VAE encoder and frozen VAE decoder. (b) PixelMatte embeds the noisy matte, the image and the trimap as pixel tokens on shared grid and predicts the matte in single forward pass without VAE. LayerShift acts inside the backbone, and the High-Pass Refiner refines the predicted matte. diffusion priors, while DRIP [20] extends latent diffusion to joint foreground and alpha prediction with dedicated transparency decoder. DiffMatte [9] instead introduces iterative pixel-level diffusion refinement using lightweight decoder, and SDMatte [10] adapts Stable Diffusion for visual-prompt-guided interactive matting. More recently, RenderMatte [33] fine-tunes FLUX.1 Kontext [13], an image-editing model pretrained on paired image-to-image data, for trimap-guided matting, combining pixel-accurate synthetic supervision with alpha-edge losses and grouprelative alignment. While these methods demonstrate the effectiveness of diffusion-based matting, approaches built upon pretrained latent image generators rely on compressed representations and decoder-based reconstruction. PixelMatte instead fine-tunes pixel-space generative backbones with the supervised recipe of RenderMatte and requires no image-editing backbone: PRXPixel is pure text-to-image model. Pixel-space diffusion transformers. Recent advances in pixel-space diffusion have demonstrated high-quality image generation without pretrained VAEs [3, 40]. JiT [19] revisits direct pixel prediction with large-patch transformers, while PixelDiT [48] combines patch-level generation with pixel-level detail modeling. PRXPixel [32] and HiDreamO1-Image [2] extend pixel-space diffusion to large-scale image generation. Beyond generation, PixRestore [38] develops pixel-space diffusion transformer trained from scratch for image restoration, incorporating feature-based conditioning for detail recovery. PixelControl [22] explores pixel-space controllable generation with additional structure-aware condition injection to improve fine-grained spatial fidelity. In contrast to these task-specific architectures, PixelMatte directly repurposes pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers for image-conditioned alpha estimation. By reusing their native patch embedding for spatially aligned image and trimap conditioning, our framework avoids additional conditioning encoders or adapters while enabling direct pixel-space matting. 3. Method Latent diffusion matting introduces representation mismatch between compressed latent features and the highfrequency precision required for image matting (Fig. 2a). In contrast, PixelMatte adapts pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers to predict and supervise alpha mattes directly in pixel space, without VAE-based reconstruction (Fig. 2b). We reuse the backbones native patch embedding to jointly process the input image, trimap, and noisy alpha matte as spatially aligned tokens (Sec. 3.1). The model is fine-tuned in two stages and performs alpha estimation in single forward pass (Sec. 3.2). Finally, LayerShift (Sec. 3.3) and the High-Pass Refiner (Sec. 3.4) further calibrate regional opacity levels and boundary transitions, respectively. 3.1. Without the subtraction, the SAD is lower on the synthetic benchmark but higher on two real test sets. 4. Experiments 4.1. Experimental Setup Implementation details. We evaluate PixelMatte with two pretrained pixel-space diffusion transformers, PRX-7B (PRXPixel [32]) and HiDream-O1-Image 8B [2]. Both follow the fine-tuning procedure of Sec. 3.2; PRX operates at 10242, while HiDream is adapted to 20482 for its final training stages and inference. PixelMatte (PRX-7B) and PixelMatte (HiDream-8B) denote the complete models with LayerShift and the High-Pass Refiner. Inference is single forward pass without test-time augmentation, and we report results averaged over two independently evaluated noise seeds. On single H200 GPU, PRX and HiDream take 0.46 at 10242 and 0.64 at 20482, respectively, compared with 0.91 for RenderMatte at 10242. [33], using their Datasets, metrics and baselines. We evaluate on P3M-500-NP [14], AM-2K [16], AIM-500 [15] and RenderMatte-2K (RM-2K) released trimaps. We report SAD, MSE (103), Grad and Conn. In Tab. 1, Conn follows the implementation released with RenderMatte for consistency with the published results; the remaining tables use the definition of DIM [44]. We compare against representative supervised and diffusion-based matting methods using the published results collected by RenderMatte [33]. 4.2. Comparison Experiments Quantitative comparison. Table 1 compares PixelMatte with existing matting methods on the four benchmarks. On P3M-500-NP and AM-2K, which are in-domain for our real-data stage, PixelMatte (HiDream-8B) reduces SAD and Grad by 3044% relative to RenderMatte, and PixelMatte (PRX-7B), which runs at the same 10242 resolution as RenderMatte, by 2438%. These gains are already evident in the one-step predictions before calibration, and the HiDream model trained only in the synthetic stage already achieves lower Grad than RenderMatte on all three realimage benchmarks. On AIM-500, both backbones reduce Grad by 2431%, indicating improved accuracy in fine spatial transitions. On the synthetic RM-2K benchmark, PixelMatte performs comparably to RenderMatte. These results show that pixel-space diffusion is an effective alternative to latent generative matting, particularly on fine structures in real images. Qualitative comparison. Figure 4 presents visual comparisons on the four benchmarks, with zoomed regions selected independently of the methods. PixelMatte recovers fine alpha structures such as hair strands and animal fur, which complements its lower gradient error. 4.3. The refiner thus calibrates boundaries already predicted by the backbone rather than re-estimating the matte from the image, with RGB providing additional benefits on real images, so the fine structures of the final matte originate from the pixel-space backbone. 4.4. Analysis and Discussion Effects of calibration. Table 4 decomposes SAD by the ground-truth alpha value and the distance to the contour. LayerShift provides modest improvements across all pixel subsets, consistent with its role in regional opacity calibration. In contrast, the High-Pass Refiner achieves its largest gains near hard boundaries: on saturated pixels within 3 px of the contour, the SAD contribution decreases from 0.54 after LayerShift to 0.23 after refinement. Figure 5 further distinguishes the two behaviors: LayerShift adjusts opacity over extended regions, whereas the High-Pass Refiner introduces localized corrections along object contours. Application to latent backbone. We further apply the same refiner architecture to RenderMatte, latent diffusion matting model; each refiner is trained on the predictions of its own backbone using only RenderMattes synthetic composite training set (Tab. 5). Both models benefit from refinement on all four benchmarks. On RM-2K, the refiner reduces the SAD of HiDream from 3.74 to 3.37 and that of RenderMatte from 3.33 to 3.28, which shows that learned boundary calibration applies to different generative matting backbones. Although direct pixel-space prediction removes the compressed latent representation and its decoder, it does not remove the limitations of generative pretraining or of matting supervision. PixelMatte inherits visual priors learned primarily for image synthesis, which may not fully capture the opacity characteristics of challenging materials: we observe residual low-amplitude alpha in saturated regions on RM-2K and noise-seed sensitivity for some transparent objects on AIM-500. Our calibration modules, which are trained separately for each backbone, improve regional opacity and boundary transitions but do not resolve every such error. 5. Conclusion We presented PixelMatte, demonstrating that pretrained pixel-space diffusion models can be effectively adapted to high-fidelity image matting through simple spatially aligned conditioning and task-specific supervision. By directly predicting alpha mattes in pixel space, our approach avoids VAE-based reconstruction while retaining the visual priors acquired during generative pretraining. Lightweight 8 opacity and boundary calibration modules further improve prediction fidelity, yielding strong results across two distinct diffusion backbones and multiple matting benchmarks. Our findings suggest that pixel-space generative foundation models offer promising alternative to latent diffusion for precision-sensitive dense prediction tasks, extending their potential beyond image synthesis.
